summary: This program looks for the cheapest and most expensive product in the "Craft" category using stream `min` and `max`, then shows three different ways to deal with the `Optional` result those methods return.

lines.text: `Optional` is Java's container for "a value that might not be there," and it is what `min` and `max` hand back, since an empty stream has no minimum.
`Comparator` supplies the rule for deciding which product counts as smaller, which `min` and `max` both require.
The list starts empty here; the comments below stand in for the product-loading code from earlier in the chapter, so this run exercises the "nothing found" path through each Optional approach.
The result is stored as an `Optional`, not a `MarketProduct`, which forces you to decide what to do when no Craft item exists instead of risking a null.
Approach 1 runs the lambda only if a value is inside, and silently does nothing otherwise — the shortest option when an empty result needs no message.
Approach 2 asks the question explicitly so you can write both branches, which is what you need when the empty case deserves its own output.
`get()` unwraps the product, and calling it is only safe because `isPresent()` has already confirmed a value is there.

lines.code: MarketProduct fallback = new MarketProduct("No Craft Item", "N/A", 0.0, "Craft", "N/A", false);
lines.text: A stand-in product is built ahead of time so the third approach always has something concrete to print.
Approach 3 collapses both cases into one expression: the real product if present, otherwise the fallback, with no `if` statement at all.

lines.text: Returning `Optional` from your own method passes the "might be missing" fact on to the caller, which is exactly what the three approaches above respond to.
The filter checks for null before comparing, so a product with a missing category is skipped rather than causing a crash.
Comparing without regard to case means "craft", "Craft", and "CRAFT" all match the requested category.
`comparingDouble` builds a comparator from the price alone, and `min` walks the filtered stream to find the smallest, wrapping the answer in an `Optional`.
`max` uses the identical comparator; only the direction of the search changes, which is why the two helper methods differ by a single word.
